{{Use dmy dates|date=April 2017}}
'''Rozanne Felicity Hastings Colchester''' (née '''Medhurst''', 10 November 1922 – 17 November 2016) worked in British intelligence in the 1940s.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url=http://rollofhonour.bletchleypark.org.uk/record_attachments/252.pdf|title=Rozanne Colchester (née Medhurst)|last=|first=|date=|website=|publisher=|access-date=}}</ref>

==Early life==
Colchester was the daughter of Sir [[Charles Medhurst]], an air attaché to the British embassy in Rome, and lived in Italy as a teenager.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |title=BBC Radio 4 - Seriously..., Seriously... - The Bletchley Girls - Cracking Women |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/programmes/articles/Q3lFn2vTv9JMgxX98bRhL/the-bletchley-girls-cracking-women#:~:text=Its%20male%20boffins%20have%20been%20hailed%20as |access-date=2024-10-03 |website=BBC |language=en-GB}}</ref> Colchester met [[Benito Mussolini|Mussolini]] and [[Adolf Hitler|Hitler]] before the Second World War,<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/history/world-war-two/11308744/The-extraordinary-female-codebreakers-of-Bletchley-Park.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150104100426/http://www.telegraph.co.uk/history/world-war-two/11308744/The-extraordinary-female-codebreakers-of-Bletchley-Park.html|url-status=dead|archive-date=4 January 2015|title=The extraordinary female codebreakers of Bletchley Park|website=Telegraph.co.uk|access-date=17 April 2016}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://dangerouswomenproject.org/2016/04/09/940/|title=An Unlikely Asset|website=Dangerous Women Project|date=9 April 2016|access-date=17 April 2016}}</ref> describing Mussolini as a "horrid man".<ref name=":1" /> Her brother "Dickie" Medhurst became a Pilot Officer and died during [[Operation Market Garden]] in 1944.<ref>{{Cite web |title=C E H Medhurst_P |url=http://www.rafweb.org/Biographies/Medhurst.htm |access-date=2024-10-03 |website=www.rafweb.org}}</ref>

== Career ==
In 1941, aged 19, she joined [[Bletchley Park]] as a decoder. Her father, himself involved in intelligence, recruited her. She spoke fluent Italian which led to her joining the [[Royal Air Force|RAF]] section.<ref name=":0"/> Following a successful interview at the [[Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office|Foreign Office]] she was immediately taken on and completed two days' training delivered by [[Leonard Hooper|Joe Hooper]].<ref>{{Cite episode|url=http://www.bbc.co.uk/programmes/p02knfvz|title=Bletchley Park decoder Rozanne Colchester - BBC Radio Oxford|website=BBC|series=Howard Bentham|access-date=15 April 2016 |date=23 February 2015|time=4:22}}</ref> She was billeted in nearby Fenny Stratford.<ref name=":2">{{Cite book |last=Fry |first=Helen |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ouXXEAAAQBAJ&dq=Rozanne+Colchester&pg=PA118 |title=Women in Intelligence: The Hidden History of Two World Wars |date=2023-01-01 |publisher=Yale University Press |isbn=978-0-300-26077-9 |pages=118–119 |language=en}}</ref>

Colchester entered one of “Britain’s most secret organisations”, Bletchley Park. The majority of Bletchley Park “was based on the forensic decrypting and ordering of thousands of enemies messages”. Colchester played a massive role in the “decrypting and ordering” of the enemy's incoming hand-encrypted messages, along with many other women working alongside Colchester at Bletchley Park. Due to Colchester’s past experience of decoding skills, this helped in uncovering many of the “general patterns of communications and confirmed logistical information”.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://dangerouswomenproject.org/2016/04/09/940/|title=An Unlikely Asset - Dangerous Women Project|date=9 April 2016|publisher=|accessdate=8 March 2018}}</ref>

She personally decrypted a high-grade Italian cypher overnight in 1943, which uncovered that the Italian air force was going to leave Tripoli that morning at 4am to bomb Sicily. Due to the intelligence, Allied forces were able to shoot down the bombers before they launched their assault.<ref name=":2" />

During Colchester’s 2010 interview with ''[[The Guardian]]'' newspaper, she mentioned how the conditions during her time at Bletchley Park were “very hard”, adding to this Colchester described the work as “monotonous, sluggish work”, but stated how gradually she began to understand the coding more and more as time went on.<ref name=":3">{{cite web|url=https://www.theguardian.com/world/2010/nov/07/women-spies-second-world-war|title=Women spies in the second world war: "It was horrible and wonderful. Like a love affair"|first=Robert|last=McCrum|date=7 November 2010|website=The Guardian|accessdate=8 March 2018}}</ref> She also said that "it was so intense. There were such a lot of very clever and eccentric people shut away in the strange isolation. I remember [[Alan Turing]], he was very shy and awfully sweet. We used to have coffee after lunch in the canteen".<ref name=":2" />

After the war, she worked for the [[Secret Intelligence Service]] in an undisclosed role. She served in [[Cairo]] and [[Istanbul]] where she helped investigate the double agent [[Kim Philby]].<ref name=":3" />

==Personal life==
In 1946, she married Halsey Sparrowe Colchester, who became vicar of [[Great Tew]] and [[Little Tew]], [[Oxfordshire]], having previously been a [[Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office|Foreign Office]] diplomat and head of personnel at [[MI6]]. They had had met in Cairo. They had four sons and a daughter.<ref>The Foreign Office List and Diplomatic and Consular Year Book 1965, Harrison & Sons, 1965, p. 165</ref><ref name=":4" />

Colchester died in 2016.<ref name=":4">{{Cite web|url=https://www.independent.co.uk/news/people/obituary-the-rev-halsey-colchester-1570963.html|title = Obituary: The Rev Halsey Colchester| website=[[Independent.co.uk]] |date = 23 October 2011}}</ref>
